analysis.one_liner: Requires pulp and paper mills to stop discharging organochlorine pollution into water within five years.
analysis.headline: The Chlorine Zero Discharge Act, introduced with 37 cosponsors, never received a hearing or vote and died when the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Clean Water Act to require pulp and paper mills to stop releasing organochlorine compounds — toxic byproducts of chlorine bleaching that persist in the environment and build up in the food chain — within five years. It would also have directed the EPA to help mills switch to chlorine-free technology and to report to Congress on other organochlorine discharges. The bill never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People who drink surface water and eat fish from contaminated waters, especially around the Great Lakes and mill towns, because the bill would have ended organochlorine pollution from pulp and paper mills at the source. Fishing communities and downstream communities would also gain cleaner water.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People who drink water and eat fish

how_it_helps.text: It would have required every pulp and paper mill using chlorine to achieve zero discharge of organochlorine compounds, byproducts, and metabolites into water within five years, with permits rewritten to enforce it.
It would have directed the EPA to evaluate chlorine-free bleaching alternatives, publish a technology-transfer report, and give technical support to mills seeking to switch.

It would have required a public accounting of organochlorine discharges nationwide, listing quantities by facility and location, with recommendations from a panel including public health experts, affected citizens, labor, and industry.

analysis.who_pays: Pulp and paper mills, which would have had five years to switch to chlorine-free bleaching technology, and eventually their customers through paper prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pulp and paper mills, then paper buyers

drawbacks.text: The bill defined 'zero discharge' as absolutely no release, not even a less-than-detectable amount, an extremely strict standard that could be technically difficult and expensive for mills to meet within five years.
Conversion costs would have fallen on mills and eventually on paper prices, and mill towns dependent on pulp and paper employment would have borne adjustment risk during the transition.
The bill covered only pulp and paper mills, leaving other industrial and nonpoint sources of organochlorine discharges untouched pending a later EPA report and recommendations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health and environmental gain — eliminating persistent, bioaccumulative organochlorines such as dioxin-related compounds from mill discharge — is substantial and permanent, and the bill included EPA technical support and an 18-month alternatives study to ease the transition. The cost is real: mills would have faced a hard five-year deadline with a no-detectable-release standard, and those costs would ripple into paper prices and mill-town employment. A more gradual or technology-based standard might have balanced the two better, but the strictness of the deadline does not change that the bill's central effect was to protect water and food chains at the expense of one polluting industry's status quo.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its water subcommittee for the rest of the Congress and died without ever getting a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 5, 1995 with 37 cosponsors, all Democrats plus one Independent.
It was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then, on April 19, 1995, to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote is recorded; the bill died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pulp and paper mills came out ahead, keeping their existing bleaching processes and avoiding the cost of converting to chlorine-free technology within five years. Ordinary people gained nothing; the organochlorine discharges the bill targeted continued.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pulp and paper mills avoided conversion costs

for.name: Rep. Bill Richardson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 37 cosponsors, all Democrats plus one Independent.

for.name: 36 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the zero-discharge bill; all 36 were Democrats.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.role: House committee of jurisdiction (chaired by Rep. Bud Shuster, R-PA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on April 5, 1995 and never reported it out or scheduled it for consideration; no further action appears in the record.

against.name: House Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral and took no recorded action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 37 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's Independent; no Republican cosponsor is recorded, and the Republican-run committee never acted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would have required these mills to eliminate organochlorine discharges within five years, forcing investment in chlorine-free bleaching technology. Mills would have borne the conversion cost; the public would have gained cleaner water.
The bill targeted chlorine and other chlorinated oxidizing agents used in bleaching, so phasing out those inputs would shrink demand for chlorine sold to the paper industry.
